title: Apéry Numbers: the Central-Binomial Lower Bound and Geometric Growth
description: A self-contained, axiom-free companion to the Apéry / ζ(3) lineage. The parent BaselProblemOQ01OQ01OQ02 proves ζ(3) irrational from five axioms, one of which is an exponential UPPER bound on the Apéry numbers bₙ = ∑ C(n,k)²·C(n+k,k)² (namely bₙ ≤ 34ⁿ); the opposite, lower half of the squeeze has no axiom-free witness there. This entry supplies it. Dropping every summand except k = n gives C(2n,n)² ≤ bₙ; a short self-contained induction proves 2ⁿ ≤ C(2n,n); together these yield the geometric lower bound 4ⁿ ≤ bₙ, the sharper rate-16 bound 16ⁿ ≤ 4n²·bₙ from the central term, and the divergence (bₙ : ℝ) → ∞. The rigorous bounds bracket the exponential growth base of bₙ in [4, 34] (and [16, 34] up to a polynomial factor); the true rate is (1+√2)⁴ = 17+12√2 ≈ 33.97.

overview.historicalContext: Roger Apéry stunned the 1978 Journées Arithmétiques at Marseille-Luminy with an elementary-looking proof that ζ(3) = ∑ 1/n³ is irrational — the first new irrationality result for a zeta value at an odd integer, and still essentially the only one known. The audience was sceptical: Apéry presented cryptic recurrences with little justification, and it took Henri Cohen, Alfred van der Poorten, and others weeks to reconstruct and verify the argument, recounted in van der Poorten's famous 1979 essay 'A proof that Euler missed'. The engine of the proof is the sequence of Apéry numbers bₙ = ∑_{k≤n} C(n,k)²·C(n+k,k)² = 1, 5, 73, 1445, 33001, …, which satisfy the recurrence n³bₙ = (34n³ − 51n² + 27n − 5)bₙ₋₁ − (n−1)³bₙ₋₂ and grow like (1+√2)⁴ⁿ = (17+12√2)ⁿ ≈ 33.97ⁿ. Apéry's irrationality criterion needs both that bₙ → ∞ geometrically and that the companion linear forms bₙζ(3) − aₙ → 0 faster than the denominators lcm(1,…,n)³ ≈ 27ⁿ blow them up. The parent gallery entry formalizes the full proof but takes the growth estimate bₙ ≤ 34ⁿ as one of five axioms; this companion supplies the complementary lower bound with no axioms at all.
overview.problemStatement: Establish, axiom-free, the lower-growth half of Apéry's squeeze for the Apéry numbers $b_n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom{n}{k}^2\binom{n+k}{k}^2$: prove $\binom{2n}{n}^2\le b_n$, the geometric bound $4^n\le b_n$, the sharper rate-16 bound $16^n\le 4n^2 b_n$, and divergence $(b_n:\mathbb{R})\to\infty$, so the exponential growth base of $b_n$ is bracketed in $[4,34]$ (and $[16,34]$ up to a polynomial factor) toward its true value $(1+\sqrt2)^4=17+12\sqrt2$.
overview.proofStrategy: The whole development hangs on one elementary observation: the k = n summand of bₙ is C(n,n)²·C(2n,n)² = C(2n,n)², so dropping every other (nonnegative) term via Finset.single_le_sum already gives C(2n,n)² ≤ bₙ. The central binomial coefficient — whose size is completely understood — is thus an honest lower bound on the intricate Apéry numbers. A self-contained induction using Mathlib's recurrence (n+1)·C(2n+2,n+1) = 2(2n+1)·C(2n,n) shows 2ⁿ ≤ C(2n,n) without Stirling, and squaring yields 4ⁿ = (2ⁿ)² ≤ C(2n,n)² ≤ bₙ. Squaring instead Erdős's Bertrand-postulate bound 4ⁿ ≤ 2n·C(2n,n) sharpens this to 16ⁿ ≤ 4n²·bₙ, recovering the true exponential order 16ⁿ/πn of the central term. Finally, casting 4ⁿ ≤ bₙ to ℝ and feeding it to tendsto_atTop_mono against tendsto_pow_atTop_atTop_of_one_lt gives bₙ → ∞. The Apéry numbers are redefined locally, so none of the parent's five axioms enter the dependency graph.
keyInsights: A single summand controls the whole sum: because every Apéry term is a nonnegative integer, the k = n term C(2n,n)² alone — extracted by Finset.single_le_sum — already lower-bounds bₙ, turning a question about a hard double-binomial sum into one about the well-understood central binomial coefficient.

The crude 4ⁿ bound throws away half the exponent. The central term genuinely grows like C(2n,n)² ≈ 16ⁿ/πn, so squaring Erdős's 4ⁿ ≤ 2n·C(2n,n) recovers 16ⁿ ≤ 4n²·bₙ — the right exponential order, off the true base 17+12√2 only by the polynomial 4n² and the slack between 16 and 34.

2ⁿ ≤ C(2n,n) is proved by a purely combinatorial induction on the recurrence, deliberately avoiding Stirling's formula or any analysis — keeping the entire growth estimate inside elementary number theory and hence genuinely axiom-free.

Apéry's irrationality argument only needs bₙ → ∞ at a geometric rate from the lower side (to outrun the lcm(1,…,n)³ ≈ 27ⁿ denominators); this entry isolates exactly that qualitative fact, decoupling it from the parent's axiomatized upper bound bₙ ≤ 34ⁿ.

Verification is foundationally clean: the small-value checks b₂ = 73, b₃ = 1445 use kernel `decide` rather than native_decide, so #print axioms shows only propext / Classical.choice / Quot.sound — no Lean.ofReduceBool, no sorryAx — making 'axiom-free' a literal claim, not a badge convention.

mainTheorems.name: centralBinom_sq_le_aperyB
mainTheorems.description: Dropping every Apéry summand except the k = n term — which is exactly C(2n,n)² — gives the central-binomial lower bound C(2n,n)² ≤ bₙ.
mainTheorems.significance: The structural lower bound that all geometric bounds build on; the central binomial coefficient sits inside every Apéry number.

mainTheorems.name: four_pow_le_aperyB
mainTheorems.description: Geometric lower bound: bₙ ≥ 4ⁿ, from C(2n,n)² ≥ (2ⁿ)² = 4ⁿ.
mainTheorems.significance: Pins the lower exponential base of the Apéry numbers, the half of the irrationality squeeze missing (axiom-free) from the parent.

mainTheorems.name: sixteen_pow_le_aperyB
mainTheorems.description: Sharper rate-16 bound bₙ ≳ 16ⁿ / 4n², obtained by squaring Erdős's central-binomial bound 4ⁿ ≤ 2n·C(2n,n).
mainTheorems.significance: Captures the actual exponential order of the central term C(2n,n)² ≈ 16ⁿ/πn, far closer to the true base 17+12√2 than the crude 4ⁿ.

mainTheorems.name: two_pow_le_centralBinom
mainTheorems.description: A self-contained induction (using the central-binomial recurrence) showing the central binomial coefficient dominates 2ⁿ.
mainTheorems.significance: Supplies the clean factor needed for the 4ⁿ lower bound without invoking Stirling or analytic estimates.

mainTheorems.description: The Apéry numbers diverge to infinity, by squeezing above 4ⁿ → ∞.
mainTheorems.significance: The qualitative fact the irrationality argument needs from the lower side: bₙ → ∞ while bₙζ(3) − aₙ → 0.

sections.title: Section I: The central term and its lower bound
sections.summary: aperyB_centralTerm: the k = n summand equals C(2n,n)² (since C(n,n)=1 and C(n+n,n)=centralBinom n). centralBinom_sq_le_aperyB: Finset.single_le_sum drops every other (nonnegative) term to leave C(2n,n)² ≤ bₙ.
sections.mathContext: The $k=n$ term is $\binom{n}{n}^2\binom{2n}{n}^2=\binom{2n}{n}^2$; all terms are nonnegative, so $\binom{2n}{n}^2\le b_n$.

conclusion.summary: The geometric lower bound on the Apéry numbers — absent (axiom-free) from the parent ζ(3) file, which only bounds bₙ from above by 34ⁿ — is established here with 0 axioms and 0 sorries: C(2n,n)² ≤ bₙ, hence 4ⁿ ≤ bₙ, the sharper 16ⁿ ≤ 4n²·bₙ, and bₙ → ∞. The bounds bracket the exponential growth base of the Apéry numbers in [4, 34].
conclusion.implications: Apéry's irrationality proof for ζ(3) hinges on bₙ → ∞ (in fact growing geometrically) while bₙζ(3) − aₙ → 0 geometrically. This entry isolates and proves, assumption-free, the lower-growth fact, complementing the parent's axiomatized upper bound. The whole argument flows from the single observation that the central binomial coefficient squared is one of the Apéry summands.
